issues.legal_issue: The alleged sale below market value did not establish that the property was undersold or that the public company suffered a loss.
material_facts: The property was offered for sale through advertised tenders, and the purchaser’s offer was the highest received.
The tender process was not shown to have been manipulated or otherwise vitiated.
The prosecution did not establish the asserted guideline value for the property or prove that its market value exceeded the accepted price.
The Collector and the Commissioner of Land Administration had assessed the land at a value consistent with the accepted price, and a sale of part of the same property also supported that valuation.
The prosecution’s other sale examples involved smaller or otherwise non-comparable properties, and the evidence did not reliably establish a higher value for the buildings.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the property was sold below its market value or that the transaction caused wrongful loss; the High Court’s conclusion was a reasonably possible view.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 47-A of the Indian Stamp Act, as amended in Tamil Nadu, and the Explanation to Rule 3 of the Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments Rules, guideline values are prima facie aids and do not conclusively determine market value. The statutory explanation defines market value by reference to the price the property would fetch in an open-market sale on the date of the instrument. An unvitiated open tender and the highest bid may be evidence of market value; comparable transactions and other reliable evidence must be considered rather than treating guideline values as conclusive.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_acquittal and open_tender_advertised and accepted_bid_was_highest and tender_process_not_shown_vitiated and prosecution_failed_to_prove_higher_market_value

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_acquittal: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.open_tender_advertised: The public owner advertised the property for sale by tender.
predicates.accepted_bid_was_highest: The public owner accepted the highest bid received for the property.
predicates.tender_process_not_shown_vitiated: The evidence did not show that the tender process was manipulated or otherwise invalidated.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_prove_higher_marke: The prosecution did not reliably establish that the property’s market value exceeded the accepted price.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquittal concerns a publicly advertised tender, the highest bid was accepted, the process was not shown to be vitiated, and a higher market value was not proved, the sale is not established to have been undervalued.

issues.legal_issue: The evidence did not establish an agreement among the accused to sell or purchase the property below its value for wrongful gain or loss.
material_facts: The prosecution sought to infer a conspiracy from the conduct of the accused and the processing of government files.
The sale followed decisions of a sub-committee and the board, and the board collectively recommended the sale and its price.
The evidence did not establish a common design or a link showing agreement to cause wrongful loss or wrongful gain.
The alleged irregularities in file circulation, notings, and approval did not establish that the accused had agreed to the alleged scheme.
issues.conclusion: The charge of conspiracy was not proved.
issues.legal_principle: A conspiracy charge requires evidence from which an agreement or common design to commit the alleged offence can be established; conduct or procedural irregularities, without a link to such an agreement, do not suffice. The Court found no basis to establish the charge under Section 120-B IPC.

predicates.criminal_prosecution_for_conspiracy: The case includes a criminal charge alleging an agreement to commit an offence.
predicates.no_evidence_of_common_design: The evidence does not establish that the accused shared a common design to commit the alleged offence.
predicates.no_link_to_wrongful_gain_or_loss: The evidence does not link the alleged agreement to a plan to cause wrongful gain or wrongful loss.

issues.definition: In a prosecution alleging conspiracy, the charge is not proved when the evidence establishes neither a common design nor a link between an agreement and the alleged wrongful gain or loss.

issues.legal_issue: The property transaction did not establish criminal misconduct by obtaining a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage through corrupt or illegal means, abuse of public office, or without public interest.
material_facts: A public servant was a partner in a firm that purchased the property from a public-sector corporation.
The corporation had pursued the sale through tender processes and approved the sale under its governance procedures.
The accepted price was not proved to be below market value, and the sale was not shown to have been made against public interest.
The evidence did not establish that the public servant used public office to secure an advantage through corrupt or illegal means or by abuse of position.
issues.conclusion: The charge under Section 13(1)(d), read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act requires proof that a public servant obtained for herself or another a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage by corrupt or illegal means, by abusing her position, or, while holding office, without public interest. The Court held that a purchase at a price not shown to be below market value, through a sale not shown to be contrary to public interest, did not satisfy those requirements.

rule.if: public_corruption_prosecution and public_servant_or_beneficiary_received_property and purchase_followed_unvitiated_public_sale and no_below_market_value_proved and no_corrupt_abuse_or_public_interest_failure_proved

predicates.public_corruption_prosecution: The case is a prosecution alleging criminal misconduct by a public servant.
predicates.public_servant_or_beneficiary_received_p: A public servant or a person for whose benefit the public servant allegedly acted acquired property in the transaction.
predicates.purchase_followed_unvitiated_public_sale: The purchase followed a public sale process that was not shown to be vitiated.
predicates.no_below_market_value_proved: The evidence did not prove that the property was sold below its market value.
predicates.no_corrupt_abuse_or_public_interest_fail: The evidence did not prove that the public servant obtained the benefit by corrupt or illegal means, abuse of office, or in the absence of public interest.

issues.definition: A property acquisition does not establish this form of criminal misconduct when it followed an unvitiated public sale, below-market pricing was not proved, and corrupt abuse or absence of public interest was not proved.

issues.legal_issue: The sale did not establish dishonest or fraudulent misappropriation or conversion of property entrusted to or controlled by a public servant.
material_facts: The property belonged to a separate public-sector corporation, which owned and controlled it.
Government approval was required before the corporation could alienate the property, but the property was not entrusted to the public servant or under her dominion as owner.
The property was sold through a tender process that was not shown to be vitiated.
The evidence did not establish dishonest conversion or misappropriation.
issues.conclusion: The charge under Section 13(1)(c), read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act applies where a public servant dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or converts to personal use property entrusted to the public servant or under the public servant’s control, or allows another person to do so. The Court held that approval authority over a corporation’s proposed sale did not itself establish entrustment or dominion over the corporation’s property.

predicates.accused_lacked_entrustment_or_dominion: The accused was not entrusted with the property and did not have dominion over it as property under the accused’s control.
predicates.dishonest_conversion_not_proved: The evidence did not prove dishonest or fraudulent misappropriation or conversion of the property.

issues.definition: A misappropriation or conversion charge is not established where a separate entity owned and controlled the property, the accused lacked entrustment or dominion, and dishonest conversion was not proved.

issues.legal_issue: A non-statutory code of conduct that is not enforceable in court does not supply the legal prohibition required for the offence of a public servant unlawfully buying property.
material_facts: The public servant was a partner in a firm that purchased property from a public-sector corporation while she held public office.
The prosecution relied on a government-issued Code of Conduct directing ministers to refrain from buying or selling immovable property to or from the Government.
The Code was not statutory, was not enforceable in court, and did not prescribe a legal sanction or procedure for a breach by the Chief Minister.
The prosecution did not identify another law that prohibited the purchase or a particular civil action arising from it.
issues.conclusion: The offence under Section 169 IPC, and the related abetment charges, were not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 169 IPC requires a public servant to be legally bound not to purchase or bid for the property in question. The required prohibition must arise from law ordinarily so understood, such as an enacted law or a rule or regulation framed under law, and not merely from non-statutory executive instructions. The Court relied on Narayan v. Emperor, 11 Criminal Law Journal Reports 613, for the need for an enactment imposing the prohibition, and on Vidadala Harinadhababu v. N.T. Ramarao, AIR 1990 AP 20, for the principle that a non-statutory code of conduct is not enforceable by courts.

predicates.prosecution_for_unlawful_purchase_by_pub: The case is a prosecution alleging that a public servant unlawfully purchased or bid for property.
predicates.public_servant_purchased_property: A public servant purchased the property, directly or through another person or entity.
predicates.prohibition_resting_only_on_nonstatutory: The asserted restriction on the purchase arose only from executive guidance that was not statutory or judicially enforceable.
predicates.no_enforceable_legal_prohibition_identif: The prosecution identified no enforceable legal rule prohibiting the public servant from purchasing the property.

issues.definition: The unlawful-purchase offence is not established when a public servant bought property but the only asserted prohibition was non-statutory guidance and no enforceable legal prohibition was identified.

issues.legal_issue: The sale did not establish criminal breach of trust by a public servant where the property was owned by a separate corporation and was not entrusted to or under the dominion of the accused.
material_facts: The corporation was a separate legal entity from the Government and owned and controlled the property.
Government approval was required for the corporation to alienate the property, but the approval requirement did not give the accused dominion over the property as owner.
The evidence did not establish that the accused had been entrusted with the property or that a trust relationship existed between the accused and the corporation.
The evidence did not establish dishonest disposal or conversion of the property for personal use.
issues.conclusion: The charge under Section 409 IPC was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 405 and 409 IPC require criminal breach of trust by a public servant, including entrustment of property or dominion over it and dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use, or disposal. The Court held that supervisory or approval authority over a separate corporation’s decision to sell its property did not, without more, amount to entrustment or dominion.

issues.definition: A breach-of-trust charge against a public servant is not established when a separate entity owned the property, the accused lacked entrustment or dominion, and dishonest disposal was not proved.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal should not be disturbed in a criminal appeal where the view reached by the appellate court below is reasonably possible and the charged offences are not established.
material_facts: The appeals challenged a High Court judgment acquitting the accused after reversing convictions.
The State had not appealed the acquittals.
The Supreme Court found that the prosecution had not established the charged offences and that the High Court’s view on the evidence was reasonably possible.
The Court considered the record sufficiently to decide whether interference was warranted and declined to reappreciate the evidence further.
issues.conclusion: There was no ground to interfere with the acquittals, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: In these proceedings under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court declined to interfere with the acquittals where the prosecution had not established the offences and the High Court’s view was reasonably possible. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The case is a criminal appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_establish_charged_: The prosecution evidence did not establish the offences charged.
predicates.lower_court_view_reasonably_possible: The view taken by the court that entered the acquittal was reasonably possible on the evidence.

issues.definition: An acquittal is not disturbed in a criminal appeal when the prosecution failed to establish the charged offences and the lower court’s view was reasonably possible.
